Pregnancy

Ostrich meat in pregnancy: nutrition, safety and claims to question

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Ostrich meat is less familiar than beef or chicken in many households, so questions about eating it during pregnancy are understandable. Its lean protein and iron content can be relevant to a meal plan. Those qualities do not establish special pregnancy benefits or remove the need to check sourcing, preparation and local food-safety advice.

A conditional food choice, not a special pregnancy treatment

There is no basis here for calling every serving of ostrich meat completely risk-free during pregnancy. Guidance commonly addresses meat and poultry in general rather than testing every species separately. Applying that guidance to a regulated, farmed ostrich product is a practical inference, not proof from a dedicated pregnancy trial.

If you choose it, use traceable muscle meat from a reputable food supplier and follow pregnancy-appropriate handling and cooking advice. Avoid raw or undercooked preparations. Ask your maternity team or local food-safety service if the origin or instructions are unclear; familiar alternatives can provide the same broad nutrient groups.

Take care with meat sold as game. NHS guidance advises avoiding game meats during pregnancy because they may contain lead, and the Food Standards Agency specifically cautions about game birds. Do not assume an unfamiliar product is exempt just because it is described as lean. This article does not clear lead-shot meat for pregnancy.

Ostrich liver is a separate food. Pregnancy guidance advises avoiding liver and liver products because of their concentrated preformed vitamin A. A discussion of muscle meat should not be used as permission to eat liver.

Why ostrich meat looks and tastes different

Ostriches are large flightless birds raised commercially alongside other sources of animal protein. Their meat may be sold as steaks, fillets, roasts or mince. Other products include leather, feathers and oils, but uses of the bird outside the kitchen say little about the safety or benefit of eating its meat.

Although the ostrich is a bird, its muscle meat is dark red and is often described in cooking as a red meat. Myoglobin, a protein involved in handling oxygen in muscle, contributes to this colour. Muscles used for sustained activity have different characteristics from the pale breast meat familiar from some poultry.

Its flavour is often compared with lean beef. The visual resemblance does not mean every beef cooking instruction or nutritional value can be transferred unchanged to ostrich. Check the actual product and its preparation instructions.

What its nutritional profile can offer

Ostrich meat provides protein and can contribute iron, zinc and B vitamins. Studies of particular cuts have found low intramuscular fat and relatively favourable iron or sodium values compared with some other meats. This can make it an interesting option within a varied diet.

However, an exact claim such as “66% less cholesterol”, or that every serving has several times the B vitamins or fatty acids of beef, needs a defined comparator and reliable measurements. Cut, animal feeding, raw versus cooked weight and recipe ingredients all affect the comparison.

It is also misleading to move directly from low total fat to a claim of abundant omega-3. The proportion of a fatty acid within a small fat content is different from the amount in a serving. Ostrich meat is not a substitute for following your maternity team’s overall nutrition advice, including appropriate sources of essential fats.

A plain fresh cut and a processed product containing added salt or fat can have quite different profiles. Look at the ingredients and the rest of the meal rather than choosing solely by the animal’s name.

Traditional claims and their limits

Some traditional food systems describe ostrich meat as warming and drying. These are cultural categories rather than measurements used to assess pregnancy nutrition or medicine. They do not establish that a food will treat a symptom.

Claims associated with this meat include antioxidant effects, stronger immunity or nerves, improved memory, a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease, and relief of stress, anxiety or depression. Other claims suggest protection against cancer or heart disease. Food-composition research does not demonstrate these clinical outcomes in people.

The same caution applies to suggested treatment of gout or other joint pain, sciatica, tremor or paralysis. Claims about better sporting endurance, general strength, faster wound healing, improved fertility or low sexual desire also require direct evidence of benefit, not just the presence of nutrients.

Iron intake and digestive comfort deserve discussion in their own right, but they should not be folded into a broad list of diseases supposedly treated by one meat. Do not stop a prescribed treatment or delay assessment in order to try it. New neurological symptoms or significant mental-health concerns need appropriate care.

Iron and anaemia during pregnancy

Pregnancy increases iron needs, and iron-containing foods can help meet them. Ostrich muscle meat is one possible source if it meets the food-safety conditions above. You do not need to eat liver to obtain iron, and other suitable meats, pulses and fortified foods can also contribute.

This is different from saying that a serving treats anaemia. Low haemoglobin or low iron stores may need investigation, an iron supplement and follow-up. Ask your maternity team what your blood-test result means and follow the treatment plan rather than replacing it with a particular food.

Protein and iron content also do not justify a blanket statement that every other organ meat is forbidden for the same reason as liver. Different organs and products need their own assessment. When planning meals, it is usually simpler to choose well-understood iron sources that fit local pregnancy guidance.

Bloating and digestion

Bloating, fullness and heartburn are common during pregnancy and can be uncomfortable or embarrassing. Eating ostrich meat has not been established in the references checked here as a treatment for gas or indigestion. A tender texture does not guarantee easier digestion for every person.

Portion size, added fat, spices and your own symptom pattern may matter more than switching meat species. Smaller meals and staying upright after eating can help some people with pregnancy-related indigestion. Ask for advice if symptoms persist; suitable medicines are available.

If a food repeatedly worsens your symptoms, choose another option and discuss persistent discomfort with your maternity team. Difficulty swallowing, unexplained weight loss or ongoing abdominal pain should not be dismissed as ordinary indigestion.

Fetal development and existing health conditions

Protein, B vitamins and essential fats all contribute to a nutritionally adequate pregnancy diet. That does not show that ostrich meat increases a baby’s intelligence, accelerates neurological development or produces a better outcome than another balanced diet. Claims based on nutrient content are not the same as trials of those outcomes.

For someone with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease or concerns about pregnancy weight gain, a lean unprocessed protein may fit an individual meal plan. It does not treat those conditions. Added salt, sauces, portion size, the other foods eaten and any prescribed medicines still matter.

Review the complete eating pattern with the maternity team or dietitian. There is no need to pursue the lowest-fat food at every meal, to restrict intake without guidance or to buy a particular meat as protection against pregnancy complications.

Buying, cooking and storing it

Keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat foods, wash hands and utensils after handling it, and keep it chilled according to the label. Thaw safely and do not leave perishable food out while preparing other dishes. Use clean utensils and plates for the cooked meat.

Use a food thermometer and the cooking instructions appropriate to the product and your country. USDA ratite guidance specifies at least 71.1°C (160°F) for ground ostrich meat. General recommendations for whole cuts may differ from pregnancy advice or the package instructions; do not use a restaurant preference for rare meat as your safety standard.

Cool and refrigerate leftovers promptly, then reheat them thoroughly according to local food-safety advice. Neither a low-fat profile nor an assumption that parasites are uncommon removes the possibility of foodborne illness from mishandled or inadequately cooked meat.

Tenderness, portions and when to seek advice

Ostrich is often lean, so prolonged dry cooking can make it tough. A moist cooking method, suitable sauce or careful timing can help preserve a pleasant texture while still reaching the required temperature. Undercooking is not a solution to dryness.

Choose an ordinary portion within a varied meal and adjust to appetite and tolerance. The available composition studies do not establish an ostrich-specific pregnancy serving size or guarantee the absence of adverse effects.

Seek medical advice if you become unwell after eating, particularly with fever, persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, dehydration or significant abdominal pain. If you are worried about a poorly cooked meal, describe what you ate and when to your maternity team rather than relying on a general claim that this meat cannot carry infection.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pregnancy guidance emphasizes safe sourcing, handling and adequate cooking of meat; it does not establish special benefits for every species.

Liver and liver products have separate pregnancy restrictions, and game provenance matters because of possible lead exposure.

Food-composition measurements do not prove treatment of digestive symptoms or improved fetal intelligence.

How BeMama can help

If you want to try an unfamiliar meat, check its source and cooking instructions first, then consider how it fits your usual meals and any maternity diet plan.

When to seek help

Avoid raw or undercooked meat and follow local advice about game and liver. Contact your maternity team if you feel unwell after eating or need help assessing an uncertain product.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ostrich muscle meat is a conditional food choice, not a proven pregnancy remedy.
  • Nutritional comparisons vary by cut and preparation.
  • Claims about intelligence, fertility, mood or disease treatment exceed what composition studies establish.
  • Cook safely even when trying to preserve tenderness, and keep liver advice separate.

Frequently asked questions

Is ostrich meat completely safe during pregnancy?

No food can be given that guarantee. For farmed muscle meat, suitability depends on sourcing, safe handling, proper cooking and local pregnancy guidance. The references do not provide a dedicated ostrich pregnancy safety trial.

What are its proposed traditional benefits?

Claims range from memory, mood and immune effects to relief of joint pain, gas or fatigue. These should not be treated as proven therapies or reasons to replace clinical care.

Can it help me get iron?

It can contribute iron as part of a suitable varied diet. Diagnosed iron deficiency or anaemia may still need supplements and follow-up; do not use meat instead of prescribed treatment.

Will it make my baby more intelligent?

That has not been established. Nutrients support normal development, but their presence in one meat does not prove an additional effect on intelligence.

Does it relieve bloating?

There is no established treatment effect in the references checked here. Meal size, recipe and individual tolerance can influence comfort; ask for help with persistent symptoms.

Can long cooking make it tough?

Yes, lean meat can dry out. Use a suitable cooking method and thermometer rather than deliberately undercooking it to preserve softness.

Does this advice also apply to ostrich liver?

No. Liver is a different product, and pregnancy guidance advises avoiding liver and liver products because of preformed vitamin A.

Is it automatically ideal for diabetes or high blood pressure?

No. A lean unprocessed protein may fit your plan, but the overall meal, salt, portions and clinical treatment still matter. Review choices with your maternity team.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
